doc.title: Lexical
doc.paragraph: The Lexical analyzer for Adaptive Framework is responsible for tokenizing Adaptive Scripts, Templates and Expressions as inputs for the parser. In this section, we will cover comments and whitespace, identifiers, keywords, operators, and literals.
The following are examples of both types of comments:
Whitespace are character sequences that are ignored by the lexical analyzer and serve the purpose of making code more readable. The following is a list of whitespace characters:

list.item: TAB character
Vertical Tab
Line Feed
Form Feed
Carriage Return
Zero Width No-Break Space
Space Separator
(Comments)

doc.paragraph: Identifiers are sequences of characters that are used to identify a variable name, category, function name, method name, parameter name, qualifier name symbol reference, interface name, type variable name, or object property name.
Identifiers have no length limit and are case-sensitive.
doc.code: Identifier ::= IdentifierStart IdentifierContinue* IdentifierStart ::= ID_START | '$' | '_' IdentifierContinue ::= ID_CONTINUE | '$' | ZWNJ | ZWJ

list.item: ID_START is any codepoint with ID_START flag
ID_CONTINUE is any codepoint with ID_CONTINUE flag
ZWNJ is the Zero-width Non-Joiner (0x200c)
ZWJ is the Zero-width Joiner (0x200d)

doc.paragraph: Separately, the lexical analyzer recognizes pound_identifier tokens: a leading # followed by an identifier-like name (for example #block or #compile). You may see them in decompile output; they are not ordinary identifiers and cannot be used as variable names. Most are not something you write in normal scripts (see Language Features); policy forms such as #compile are the exception.
When declaring a variable name, you may use any identifier with the exception of the following reserved names:
doc.code: false INF Infinity NaN null true undefined break case catch const continue default do else extends finally for function if interface let return switch throw try type void while as async await class delete export from import in instanceof super this typeof var with
doc.paragraph: Literals are constant that can be used as a values inside expressions. There are three types of literals:

list.item: Array Literal
Object Literal
Scalar Literal

doc.paragraph: A Array Literal is a sequence of literals, separated by , and enclosed in [ and ].
An Object Literal is a sequence of Identifier : Literal pairs, separated by , and enclosed by { and }.
A Scalar Literal may be one of: Double, Integer, String, true, false or null.

Adaptive Script regular expressions are . Like everything else in AFW, they work on Unicode text: a pattern matches code points, not UTF-16 code units, so an emoji or any character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is one character and never half of one. Classes such as \w, \d, and \b, and case-insensitive matching, follow Unicode for every language, and matching reads AFW's UTF-8 strings directly, without converting them. The syntax will look familiar from ECMAScript, Perl, and Java. Where ICU's Unicode rules give a different answer than ECMAScript or XML Schema regular expressions, the notes at the end of this section say what to write.

section.title: Writing a Pattern
section.paragraph: A regular expression literal is written as in ECMAScript, where a value can start: /pattern/flags. Its value has data type regexp and is compiled once, when the script is compiled, so a pattern that does not compile is a syntax error at the literal, and using it costs no compile at run time. The pattern is passed to ICU as written: backslashes are not doubled. Write a / in the pattern as \/ or inside a class ([/]). After a value, / divides, and /= always divides and assigns.
The typed literal "a+b"re (or "a+b"regexp) is the same value, written as a string, so its backslashes are doubled: "\\d+"re is /\d+/.
A pattern matches anywhere in the value unless ^ and $ anchor it: regexp_match("xaab", /a+b/) is true and regexp_match("xaab", /^a+b$/) is false.

section.title: Flags

list.item: i ignores case, using Unicode case folding.
m lets ^ and $ match at the start and end of each line.
s lets . match a line terminator.
x ignores whitespace and # comments in the pattern.
u is accepted and changes nothing: patterns are always Unicode.

section.paragraph: Flags become part of the pattern: /a+b/i is "(?i)a+b"re. There is no g flag; regexp_replace takes a limit instead.

section.title: Functions
section.paragraph: The regexp functions take a regexp, not a string: regexp_match(value, regexp), regexp_index_of(value, regexp) (the code point index of the first match, or -1, counted as index_of counts), and regexp_replace(value, regexp, replacement, limit?) (limit 1 by default, -1 for every match). In the replacement, $1 is the text of group 1, $0 the whole match, ${name} a named group, and a backslash makes the next character literal (\$).

To use a pattern you have as a string, convert it once with to_regexp(s) and keep the result. A regexp value read from data is compiled each time a function uses it, unless you compile it once with compile<regexp>(r).
section.code: const date = /(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d\d)-(?<d>\d\d)/; regexp_replace("2024-10-13", date, "${d}/${m}/${y}"); // "13/10/2024" regexp_replace("a1b22c333", /\d+/, "#", -1); // "a#b#c#" regexp_index_of("xyzaab", /a+b/); // 3 regexp_match("Ελλάδα", /^\w+$/); // true

section.title: Match Limit
section.paragraph: ICU finds a match by backtracking, so some patterns, such as /^(a+)+$/ on a long run of a that does not end the way the pattern expects, take time that grows exponentially with the length of the value. A match stops after a fixed number of steps of the ICU match engine with a payload_too_large error, so a pattern, even one that arrives in a request, cannot hold a thread. The number is the process limit limitRegexpMatchSteps: 1000 by default, about a tenth of a second of backtracking, and far more than a linear scan of a long value needs. An application conf can change it like the other limit* settings (0 is unlimited), and process::limitRegexpMatchSteps shows the current value.

Because of an ICU issue, a lazy loop over a group that can match nothing, such as (b|)*? or (a?)+?, can reach the limit even on a short value. Write the loop so its body cannot match empty: b*? instead of (b|)*?.

section.title: Coming from ECMAScript
section.paragraph: ECMAScript keeps some rules for compatibility with its first, ASCII and UTF-16 days. AFW does not need them, so these give a different answer than ECMAScript:

list.item: \d, \w, and \b are Unicode: é is a word character and ٣ is a digit. For ASCII only, write [0-9] or [A-Za-z0-9_].
The i flag uses full Unicode case folding: /strasse/i matches "Straße".
Without the m flag, $ also matches just before a line terminator at the end of the value: regexp_match("ab\n", /^ab$/) is true. Write \z for the very end.
The line terminators are LF, CR, CR LF, U+0085, U+2028, and U+2029, so . does not match U+0085.
[^] is a syntax error. Write [\s\S], or use the s flag.
A lookbehind must have a bounded length.
In a replacement, write $0 for the whole match (ECMAScript $&), ${name} for a named group ($<name>), and \$ for a dollar sign ($$).
There are no g, y, d, or v flags. Use the limit of regexp_replace for every match.
ICU also has things ECMAScript does not, such as \A, \z, \Z, the x flag, inline flags (?i), atomic groups (?>...), and possessive quantifiers a*+.

section.title: Coming from XML Schema Regular Expressions and fn:matches
section.paragraph: Earlier versions of AFW used XML Schema regular expressions. XPath fn:matches uses the same syntax with ^, $, and flags added.

list.item: A pattern matches anywhere in the value, as with fn:matches. An XML Schema pattern always had to match the whole value: write ^...\z for that.
Without the m flag, $ also matches just before a line terminator at the end of the value; fn:matches matches only at the end. Write \z for the very end.

\w is letters, marks, digits, and connector punctuation (in XML Schema, every character except punctuation, separators, and other), and \s is all Unicode white space (in XML Schema, space, tab, LF, and CR only).
The m flag and . use all the ICU line terminators, not only LF and CR, and the i flag uses full case folding.
The XML name escapes \i and \c are not ICU syntax, and class subtraction is written [a-z--[aeiou]] instead of [a-z-[aeiou]].
ICU also accepts lookahead, lookbehind, named groups, \b, and lazy and possessive quantifiers.
